chapter: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
title: A concert with young musicians; Marshall Royal; Ellington's timelessness
summary: After a concert with Jimmy Jones, Collins and Marshall Royal agree old timers must show the kids, and he cites Ellington's vigor.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: But I had my group, Jimmy Jones on piano, and Harold Jones on drums and Jim [Hewitt] bass, and we went out and we played. And the response was resounding. So after we finished I went to the dressing room and everyone, the kids and the older musicians, said, oh, that was just so beautiful. And I looked over there and sitting on the couch was Marshall Royal, who was going to appear with the [pier] band that came on later. And it occurred to me we have to show the kids.

I looked at Marshall and I said now here's a great saxophone player, this is -- we have to -- and I said this to Marshall, I said, well Marshall, you know, we old timers really have to do something for the kids. He said, that's right. You know, because it's timeless, you know. You don't grow old musically. I don't think so. I know better.

Like Duke Ellington. Duke Ellington was timeless. Here's a man that actually had to slow up sometimes so the people could catch up to what he was doing. This man was just that great, and he was just as -- his music was as vigorous, as innovative when he died as it ever was. He was abreast of everything, he was right with it. So this was the only way you -- how can you analyze this. You know.
